..
Issued at 241 PM EDT Wed Jul 29 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Large scale thermal ridge axis remains over the western Plains and 
the eastern Front Range of the Rockies, with a wave over New England 
actively closing off. This leaves northern lower and eastern upper 
Michigan in the grip of a progressive flow regime, and quick moving 
shortwave features. Current shortwave ridge axis overhead coinciding 
with 500mb height rises and a broad 1017mb area of surface high 
pressure stretching from James Bay through the Ozarks. With this 
area of surface high pressure passing overhead, subsidence and lack 
of deeper moisture will suppress convective tendencies outside of 
some diurnally driven cumulus clouds through Thursday. Already 
seeing the budding stages of the next wave set to crest the ridge 
axis after monsoonal convection manifests over the eastern Great 
Basin into WY / ID. 

Anticipation is that this wave comes with a modest convective charge 
across the western Corn Belt Thursday. As the wave approaches, 
aforementioned wave over New England set to have been ingested by 
broader longwave trough over Atlantic Canada. Result will be a turn 
of flow to more northerly over the Great Lakes. As such, the 
approaching wave from the west will likely be forced a bit more 
southerly Friday into Saturday. Current trends support this more 
southerly turn with this ensuing wave to focus any vigorous 
convective responses to our south and west, and thus limiting deeper 
moisture (widespread 70+ surface dewpoints) from reaching the 
region. Nonetheless, with return flow providing enough moisture to 
support scattered convection Friday and into Saturday. In the wake 
of this wave, anticipating another round of 500mb height rises to 
suppress rain chances heading into early next week, with guidance 
perhaps hinting at another wave approaching some time toward the end 
of or perhaps just beyond the current forecast period.

Details: 

Dry and Seasonably Warm Today; A Touch More Humid Thursday: Surface 
high pressure really puts a lid on sensible weather across the 
region the next couple days. Mostly sunny skies to prevail, aside 
from some afternoon diurnal cumulus clouds. Temperatures will be 
seasonable to slightly above normal for late July. Highs peak in the 
mid 70s to low 80s today, with overnight lows in the 55-65 range 
tonight. More of the same into Thursday, however, subtle moisture 
plume associated with the incoming wave may try to start leaking 
into the region, which may force dewpoints to approach 60 during the 
day, adding a touch more noticeable humidity to the region. Warming 
temps aloft should nonetheless allow for a warmer day at the surface 
with continued efficient mixing, ranging 80 to 88. For the time 
being, these warmer temperatures aloft should keep us capped, but 
will have to see how strong the cap is. Lake breezes will likely be 
active, so suppose there is potential for some convection in 
northeast lower; however, guidance isn't exactly enthusiastic about 
the idea with continued subsidence overhead, so will opt to leave 
this out of the forecast./. will note increasing SREF PoP trends, so 
entirely possible a shower or two gets added into the next forecast 
cycle or two. A touch more warmth overnight Thursday into Friday... 
with overnight lows Thursday night probably settling into the low-to-
upper 60s for most... perhaps some upper 50s in the interior terrain 
of northeast lower where return flow will be weakest Thursday night.

Rain Chances: Next wave set to approach the region Friday and into 
Saturday as the 500mb trough axis traverses the Great Lakes. 
Aforementioned southerly dive in the track of this wave will be 
detrimental to us seeing widespread rainfall, as deeper moisture 
and more robust thunderstorm development parameters favor areas just 
SW of the Great Lakes. Nonetheless, the intrusion of moisture and 
subtly steeper lapse rates aloft may be just enough to support some 
mesoscale driven shenanigans up yonder... with southerly return flow 
anticipated Friday, may need to watch for any lake breeze generated 
convection over northeast lower during the day before any stratiform 
/ weaker convective rains build Friday night into Saturday. 
Certainly not looking like a widespread washout across the region, 
with plenty of dry time into Saturday, but enough to inconvenience 
summer leisure activities at times. Again, this does not look like a 
widespread rain by any means... and the lack of deeper moisture may 
leave much to be desired in the rainfall department. Genuinely would 
not surprise me if some areas didn't receive any rainfall. Following 
the passage of this wave, we look to dry out by Sunday, with the 
next rain chance perhaps returning at the very end of the forecast 
pattern, or the middle of next week.
